newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. defence secretary in Korea, meets Shalikashvili.
newsitem.headline: U.S. defence secretary in Korea, meets Shalikashvili.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretry William Cohen said on Wednesday there were growing signs of a severe food crisis in North Korea and urged Pyongyang to work with the United States and South Korea to solve the problem.

Cohen also stressed to reporters on arrival from Japan for security talks with South Korean President Kim Young-sam and others that a dispute between Seoul and Washington over the possible sale of Russian anti-aircraft missiles to South Korea would not damage the U.S.-South Korea alliance.

The secretary, on the last leg of a Pacific trip, met for about 45 minutes at his hotel with U.S. Army General John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Pentagon Joint Chiefs of Staff, who was winding up a visit to South Korea before going to Japan on Thursday.

"I think the evidence is mounting that it (hunger in North Korea) appears to be very severe and that hopefully it will allow us to (go ahead) with the four-party (peace) talks in the very near future," he said of proposed talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China.

"We are looking for greater visibility, transparency ... finding out whether there is a willingness on the part of the North Koreans in conjunction with their South Korean counterparts to solve the crisis," Cohen told reporters aboard his aircraft en route from Tokyo.
North Korea is expected to respond on April 16 to the four-nation talks proposed by the United States and South Korea, a Seoul government official said on Wednesday.
The talks aim to formally end the 1950-53 Korean War.

Cohen, who will visit U.S. troops along the heavily fortified demilitarised zone (DMZ) between North and South Korea on Thursday, repeated Washington's fears that the food crisis could prompt North Korea's 1.1 million-strong military to revolt against its government or strike out against the South.

"We have no way of predicting that right now and so what we have to have is a very strong deterrent capability plus a willingness to work with the South Koreans to solve this crisis," he told reporters.
The United States has 37,000 troops in South Korea and Cohen caused a stir this week when he said they would remain in Korea indefinitely even if the two Koreas made peace and united.
Cohen said Washington was moving cautiously on food aid for the North and that it would be handled only in conjunction with South Korea and other countries.
"We will work very closely with our South Korean allies to see where we go from here," Cohen said.

Speaking with reporters on his aircraft, Cohen appeared to soften his earlier warning that South Korea would be making a major military and political mistake if it bought Russian SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles instead of U.S. Patriots.
"I think that our relationship is going to remain durable without regard to the sale, should it occur," he said when asked if Seoul's purchase of Russian missiles would damage ties.
"We have made the case that we would like to see greater inter-operability with our systems, but in spite of that we will continue to maintain a strong relationship with the South Koreans."

Cohen earlier said that he objected to the sale because the Russian missiles might threaten U.S. warplanes in the confusion of any new Korean war. He and other U.S. officials said the missiles lacked electronic safeguards that would allow them to identify U.S. planes as friendly to South Korea.
Cohen was due to have dinner on Wednesday night with General John Tilelli, commander of U.S. troops in South Korea.

The secretary, who held talks in Tokyo with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Wednesday morning, will meet on Thursday with President Kim, Defence Minister Kim Dong-jin and Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha.
